Search results lean toward Better Auth for new projects, with Clerk and Auth.js positioned as narrower choices. The sources are mostly vendor-affiliated blogs, so treat them as opinion.

- **Better Auth:** The sources describe it as a self-hosted TypeScript library that stores users in your own database. One says it launched in 2024 and reached v1.6 in May 2026. A competitor's comparison credits it with a broad built-in feature set, including 2FA, passkeys, RBAC, impersonation, and more. The main drawback is that you own security updates.
- **Auth.js (NextAuth v5):** One source reports that the Better Auth team took over Auth.js maintenance, and the library is in security-patch mode. It adds that the Auth.js team's own guidance for new projects points to Better Auth. Existing Auth.js apps keep working, so this mainly matters for new projects. I found this claim in only one source, so verify it before relying on it.
- **Clerk:** It is a hosted service where the session store, user database, and JWT signing keys all live in Clerk's infrastructure. Its pricing starts with a free tier, and one source notes it gets expensive past 50,000 MAU and locks your user data in a US database. Its pre-built UI and fast setup are its main strength.

Overall, the sources suggest Better Auth for self-owned, cost-controlled SaaS, Clerk for speed with less infrastructure work, and Auth.js mainly for existing apps. Three results were low-quality keyword pages with no real content, so I ignored them.

title: proxy.js
description: API reference for the proxy.js file.
related:
  title: Learn more about Proxy
  links:
    - app/api-reference/functions/next-request
    - app/api-reference/functions/next-response
---

> **Note**: The `middleware` file convention is deprecated and has been renamed to `proxy`. See [Migration to Proxy](#migration-to-proxy) for more details.

The `proxy.js|ts` file is used to write [Proxy](/docs/app/getting-started/proxy) and run code on the server before a request is completed. Then, based on the incoming request, you can modify the response by rewriting, redirecting, modifying the request or response headers, or responding directly.

Proxy executes before routes are rendered. It's particularly useful for implementing custom server-side logic like authentication, logging, or handling redirects.

> **Good to know**:
>
> Proxy is meant to be invoked separately of your render code and in optimized cases deployed to your CDN for fast redirect/rewrite handling, you should not attempt relying on shared modules or globals.
>
> To pass information from Proxy to your application, use [headers](#setting-headers), [cookies](#using-cookies), [rewrites](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-response#rewrite), [redirects](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-response#redirect), or the URL.

Create a `proxy.ts` (or `.js`) file in the project root, or inside `src` if applicable, so that it is located at the same level as `pages` or `app`.

If you’ve customized [`pageExtensions`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/pageExtensions), for example to `.page.ts` or `.page.js`, name your file `proxy.page.ts` or `proxy.page.js` accordingly.

```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'

// This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
  return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
}

export const config = {
  matcher: '/about/:path*',
}
```

```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'

// This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside

  return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
}

export const config = {
  matcher: '/about/:path*',
}
```

## Exports

### Proxy function

The file must export a single function, either as a default export or named `proxy`. Note that multiple proxy from the same file are not supported.

content.text:
Email/password sign-up and sign-in work, and `/dashboard` now needs a session. Google sign-in is wired up, but I only checked that it redirects to Google with the placeholder client ID. I tested the rest against the dev server with curl: anonymous access redirects, sign-up works, a wrong password is rejected, and the dashboard shows the signed-in user. `next build` passes, but I never loaded the sign-in/sign-up pages in a browser or clicked through the forms.

## Library choice
I chose **Better Auth** over Auth.js (NextAuth v5) and Clerk. The comparisons I found are mostly vendor blogs, so treat them as opinion.
- **Better Auth:** it's self-hosted and keeps users in your own database. It has no per-user pricing and supports email/password and Google out of the box. The sources point to it as the pick for new projects.
- **Auth.js:** one source says it is now in security-patch mode, with its team pointing new projects to Better Auth. That came from a single source and I didn't verify it.
- **Clerk:** it's hosted and fast to set up, but your user data lives with them and costs rise at scale. I didn't want a paid external dependency for this.

Sources: [supastarter](https://supastarter.dev/blog/better-auth-vs-nextauth-vs-clerk), [makerkit](https://makerkit.dev/blog/tutorials/better-auth-vs-clerk), [LogRocket](https://blog.logrocket.com/best-auth-library-nextjs-2026/), [turbostarter](https://www.turbostarter.dev/blog/better-auth-vs-clerk-vs-nextauth-vs-supabase-auth)

## What changed
- **Storage:** I used a local SQLite file (`better-sqlite3`, default `data/notely.db`, gitignored). It's not suited to serverless hosting, so switch the database in `src/lib/db.ts` before deploying there.
- **Auth setup:** `src/lib/auth.ts` configures Better Auth, `src/lib/auth-client.ts` is the browser client, and `src/app/api/auth/[...all]/route.ts` is the handler.
- **Route protection:** `src/proxy.ts` redirects to `/sign-in` when there is no session cookie. This is only a cookie-presence check, so the dashboard page also validates the session and redirects if it is invalid.
- **`src/lib/users.ts`:**
  - `getCurrentUser()` now returns the user from the real session.
  - `listUsers()` and `getUser()` read the auth `user` table.
  - I removed the hardcoded Ada and Grace users, since they had no passwords.
- **UI:** `/sign-in` and `/sign-up` pages, a Google button, a sign-out button on the dashboard, and a `next` redirect that only accepts same-site paths.
- **Credentials:** placeholders are in `.env.example`, and I added a `.gitignore` exception so it can be committed.

## To run it
1. `cp .env.example .env.local`, then set `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` (`openssl rand -base64 32`).
2. Create a Google OAuth client with redirect URI `http://localhost:3000/api/auth/callback/google`, and fill in `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` and `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET`.
3. `npm run db:migrate` creates the tables. I added this script.
4. `npm run dev`

## Heads-up
- `BETTER_AUTH_URL` must match the origin you browse from. Better Auth rejected my first test run on port 3100 with "Invalid origin" until I used 3000.
- `tsc` reports `Cannot find name 'LayoutProps'` in `layout.tsx`. That error comes from the original scaffold, and `next build` passes.
- `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` showed up as untracked files. I didn't create them, so check whether you want them.
- Nothing is committed.
